items.titleOriginal: Argentina court orders return of Nazi-looted Old Master portrait to Jewish dealer’s heir
items.summaryKo: Lawyers for the heir, a descendant of the Dutch dealer Jacques Goudstikker, say the outcome is ‘unprecedented’ as it involves the recovery of a work held in private hands through a criminal case Giacomo Antonio Melchiorre Ceruti, Portrait of a Lady , 18th century Photo: Belén Cano, Ministerio Público Fiscal A Nazi-looted painting discovered last year in photographs from a real estate listing for a house in Argentina will be restituted to Marei von Saher, heir to the Dutch Jewish art. dealer Jacques Goudstikker , in a case her lawyers say is virtually unprecedented because the work was recovered from private hands through criminal proceedings. Portrait of a Lady , an 18th-century painting by Giacomo Antonio Melchiorre Ceruti (previously attributed to Giuseppe Ghislandi) valued at around €250,000, had remained for decades in the possession of the family of Friedrich Kadgien, an official in the Nazi regime who fled Europe after the Second World War and eventually settled in Mar del Plata. “As. far as we know, this is the first time that the Argentine justice system has recovered and restituted a painting looted by the Nazis during the Second World War,” Juan Ignacio Pascual, one of the Argentine lawyers representing Von Saher and the Goudstikker family, tells The Art Newspaper . Pascual worked on the case alongside the Argentine lawyers Herberto Robinson and Guillermo Brady. items.titleOriginal: 15 Museum Exhibitions to See Across the US This Fall
items.summaryKo: Tony Cokes’s riffs on the video essay, a Grandma Moses retrospective, and Abbas Akhavan’s US museum debut are among the shows to look forward to this season. The circus is coming to town, although maybe not in the form you’d expect. The art world, in all its acrobatics, pageantry, and occasional fun, is returning to cities across the United States this fall with a spate of acts. Artist Karon Davis ushers us into the big top in an exhibition rife with circus archetypes at the. Seattle Art Museum. In a group show at the Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University, we’re given front seats to the circus that is American democracy. There may be no ringmaster inside this tent, but there’s certainly showbiz: the Denver Art Museum has dedicated an entire show to the diva phenomenon, while at Virginia Commonwealth University’s Institute for Contemporary Art, Tony Cokes takes the shears to the codes of popular culture. The magic act continues elsewhere: every piece of rubbish that jewelry designer Bernhard Schobinger. touched turned into gold, as evidenced by a new show at the Museum of Fine Arts Houston. And up north, a photography exhibition at the Milwaukee Museum of Art pairs the alchemy of resource extraction with that of photography, a comparison that needs no smoke and mirrors, save for the one in a DSLR camera. — Phillip Pyle, associate editor Read our 2026 fall guides for New York and Los Angeles . Nasher Museum of Art , Duke University, Durham, North Carolina Aug. 27–July 11, 2027.

items.titleOriginal: Preserving Ernie Barnes’s Legacy in Paint Tubes
items.summaryKo: The late artist and athlete who rendered joyous scenes of Black life, dance, and motion is the subject of renewed institutional attention as his daughter, Erin Barnes, works to conserve his studio practice. When artist Ernie Barnes died in 2009, his daughter Erin was left to sort through the vestiges of materials the Los Angeles-based painter and professional football player had accumulated over his decades-long art practice. There were canvases, sure, but also paint tubes, brushes, and containers Barnes kept. in the garage that he used as his studio to create vibrant, kinetic scenes of Black church gatherings, football games, and nightlife during the Jim Crow era, including his iconic work “ The Sugar Shack ” (1976), making him one of Southern California’s most beloved artists. For years, Barnes stored her father’s partially squeezed containers of Liquitex, Grumbacher, and Winsor & Newton acrylic paint and thought little about it until about a year ago, when she began to realize the. materials were integral to commemorating his legacy. “I realized how much of the physical studio still existed through the paint tubes and brushes, and I felt a responsibility to preserve them as part of a record of his historical practice,” Barnes told Hyperallergic . “These tubes are the physical remnants of his creative process.” Black figurative painters such as Jacob Lawrence, Amy Sherald, and Kerry James Marshall have been widely celebrated by museums and institutions in the last decade. items.titleOriginal: The Artist Residency That Never Was
items.summaryKo: Abstract Mag invited dozens of artists to participate in a summer residency in Georgia. Then its social media pages went dark. Like hundreds of other visual artists around the world, 25-year-old airbrush painter Syd Sauer Wilson opened their email inbox on Friday, June 5, to what appeared to be the opportunity of a lifetime: an invitation to participate in an artist residency program hosted by Abstract Mag — a popular art-focused social media platform that had over 1 million followers —. taking place overseas this summer. The residency promised an all-expenses-paid retreat in the mountainous regions of southern Georgia, where for two weeks in August, 40 visual artists would live in a “historic chateau” and pursue their practices while also exploring the country’s culture and traditions through a series of expeditions and activities. For the emerging artist hungry for any opportunity to create works in a historic environment without having to pay for travel, materials, or accommodations, a residency like this would. be a dream come true. This was the case for Wilson, an early-career artist in Los Angeles. They had applied to last year’s residency, hosted in the 18th-century Château De Forbin in Marseille, for a $40 fee after seeing the open call for artists on Abstract Mag’s social media pages.
